Inexcusable
ĭn-ĕks-kūz´a-bl
adj. (admitting of no excuse or justification; without defence)
Latin inexcusabilis, from ex-, out, and causa, a cause or plea — to excuse is to plead a man out of his charge. The AV uses the word once, at Romans 2:1.

Biblical Definition

The word appears once: “Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things” (Rom 2:1). Its companion closes the case against the pagan: God's eternal power and Godhead are seen in the things He made, “so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20). The Lord says the same of those who heard Him: “If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin” (John 15:22). The purpose of the whole indictment is stated: “that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God” (Rom 3:19). And knowledge raises the account (Luk 12:47).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines inexcusable as not to be excused or justified; as an inexcusable fault, an inexcusable neglect of duty.

expand to see more

INEXCUSABLE, a. Not to be excused or justified; as inexcusable folly.

INEXCUSABLENESS, n. The quality of not admitting of excuse or justification.

EXCUSE, v.t. To pardon; to free from the imputation of fault or blame; to acquit of guilt.

Key Scripture

Rom 2:1 — "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things."

Rom 1:20 — "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:"

John 15:22 — "If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin."

Rom 3:19 — "Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God."

Luk 12:47 — "And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes."

Modern Corruption

Romans 2:1 is read as a ban on all moral judgment, and it is an indictment of the man whose judgment is accurate.

expand to see more

The popular use of this verse gets its logic backwards. Paul does not say the moralist's verdict on the pagan was wrong; he grants it and turns it. Wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things. The problem is not that the standard was misapplied but that it was applied in one direction only, and the man who can see the fault clearly enough to name it has demonstrated that he knows the law he is breaking. Being right about someone else's sin is precisely what leaves him without a defence.

Romans 1:20 and 3:19 together explain why the doctrine matters. The whole first section of Romans is a legal argument working toward a verdict — every mouth stopped, all the world guilty before God — and it must reach that point before 3:21 can say But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested. Grace is unintelligible to a man who still has a plea. This is why preaching that never establishes guilt produces converts who are grateful for improvement rather than for rescue.

Luke 12:47 keeps the doctrine from flattening into a single verdict. The servant who knew his lord's will and did it not shall be beaten with many stripes; he that knew not, with few. Guilt is universal and it is not uniform, and the ones with most to answer for are those who sat under the clearest light. John 15:22 says the same of the men who heard Christ Himself speak: now they have no cloke for their sin. A church member of thirty years hearing sound preaching should find that sobering rather than reassuring.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anapologetos (G379), without excuse, inexcusable; prophasis (G4392), a pretext, cloke; hupodikos (G5267), under judgment, guilty; phrasso (G5420), to stop the mouth.

expand to see more

Greek anapologetos (G379) — without excuse; Romans 1:20, 2:1 — both occurrences.

Greek prophasis (G4392) — pretext, cloke; John 15:22, Matthew 23:14, 1 Thessalonians 2:5.

Greek hupodikos (G5267) — guilty, answerable; Romans 3:19 only.

Usage

"“Wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself” — the verdict was right."

"“That every mouth may be stopped” — and only then, But now."

"“They have no cloke for their sin” — of men who had heard Him."
